name: William B. Mair
tagline: Professor of Molecular Metabolism · Director, Harvard Chan Healthy Aging Initiative

glance.label: Research
glance.html: Fundamental mechanisms of metabolic flexibility, nutrient and energy sensing (AMPK, mTORC1, CRTC-1), organelle dynamics and RNA splicing in healthy aging; discovery biology in C. elegans with translation toward precision geroscience.

glance.label: Leadership
glance.html: Director, Harvard Chan Healthy Aging Initiative (2024-). Co-founding Director, MBL Biology of Aging course (2023-). Organizer, CSHL Mechanisms of Aging meeting (2022, 2024, 2026). Co-chair, Fusion Interventions in Aging (2025, 2027). Chief Scientific Advisor, The WNDR Lab (2025-).

blocks.html: I am a molecular geneticist who studies why age is the greatest risk factor for chronic disease, and how that risk can be reduced. My central hypothesis is that aging and age-related disease stem from a progressive loss of metabolic flexibility, the capacity of cells, tissues and whole organisms to respond acutely and appropriately to changes in nutrient supply, and that restoring this "homeodynamic" capacity can promote healthy aging.

As a graduate student with Linda Partridge I described the first late-onset dietary intervention to reverse mortality trajectories in Drosophila and showed that macronutrient balance, not calories, drives the longevity effect of dietary restriction. As a postdoc with Andrew Dillin I identified CRTC coactivators as direct longevity targets of the energy sensor AMPK. My own group at Harvard has since defined how AMPK and mTORC1 integrate in the nervous system to regulate systemic aging cell non-autonomously; discovered causal roles for RNA splicing factors in longevity and in individual variation in response to interventions; and established organelle plasticity, mitochondrial network dynamics, ER-mitochondrial calcium signaling and, most recently, peroxisomal function, as the effector arm through which nutrient sensors govern metabolic aging. Along the way we have built widely used genetic tools in C. elegans for single-copy knock-in, tissue-specific ribosome profiling and acute protein degradation.

The next phase is precision geroscience: defining biomarkers that predict who will respond to which intervention, and translating these mechanisms into mammalian systems and human cohorts. As Director of the Harvard Chan Healthy Aging Initiative I work to integrate the biology of aging with public health, with a particular focus on the inequities in healthy aging that make this a public-health emergency rather than a luxury problem.

sections.title: Research resources and tools shared with the community

blocks.html: SKI LODGE; single-copy knock-in loci for defined gene expression in C. elegans (Silva-García et al., G3 2019): CRISPR safe-harbor system for tissue-specific single-copy transgenes, used with auxin-inducible degradation for acute, reversible, cell-type-specific protein depletion. Strains deposited with the Caenorhabditis Genetics Center (lab code WBM) and shared directly with laboratories worldwide; pSKI vectors on Addgene.

SKI TRIP; single-copy knock-in translating ribosome immunoprecipitation toolkit for tissue-specific profiling of actively translated mRNAs (Wester et al., Cell Reports Methods 2023); strains at the CGC, datasets on Mendeley Data and SRA (PRJNA801467).
Auxin-degron alleles of the mTORC1 pathway (RAGA-1, LET-363/mTOR, Raptor, Rictor, S6K) for spatiotemporal control of nutrient signaling (Smith et al., PLoS Genetics 2023).
Mitochondrial morphology imaging toolkit; endogenous CRISPR-tagged and ectopic reporters benchmarked against conventional markers (Valera-Alberni et al., Life Science Alliance 2024).
Mito-NAD(P)H age clocks; label-free, non-destructive FLIM-based predictor of biological age and remaining lifespan at subcellular resolution (Morrow et al., Communications Biology 2024).
